en: The Chapter on the Five-Syllable Heart Dharani of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī from the Vajraśekhara Sūtra,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from the country of Mālava in South India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Translated by Vajrabodhi by Imperial Decree. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, including the Vajradhara Bodhisattva and all other bodhisattvas, were all before the Buddha Vairocana.
Each [bodhisattva] spoke of their own heart-mantra and mudrā.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I too, desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, [speak this]."
Because one will swiftly attain the accomplishment of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā,
he also taught the Heart Dhāraṇī.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family! Now is precisely the time.
You should proclaim it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī—
Receiving the Buddha’s instruction, he then spoke this dhāraṇī:
"A-ra-pa-ca-na-ja. Good sons and good daughters, if there are those who can receive and uphold this dhāraṇī..."
One immediately enters the equality of all dharmas of the Tathāgata;
all syllables are likewise equal.
One will swiftly achieve the accomplishment of Mahāprajñā.
To recite it even once is equivalent to upholding all eighty-four thousand collections of sutras;
those who wish to receive and uphold it [should do so].
One should first invite them to enter the initiation maṇḍala.
On the fifteenth day of the waxing moon,
that ācārya shall prepare a circular altar in a clean room.
Having smeared the ground with sandalwood and camphor scented mud,
one should then paint Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva in the center of the maṇḍala,
in the form of a youth.
The right hand holds a vajra-sword, and the left hand holds a *mahāprajñā* palm-leaf manuscript.
Around the perimeter of the mandala circle,
the syllables A-ra-pa-ca-na are written in Sanskrit.
One should offer various kinds of fragrant incense and exquisite flowers with a devoted mind.
The ācārya, having performed the empowerment for the disciple by means of the vajra-mudrā and reciting the mantra according to the ritual rules, [concludes the rite].
Thereafter, he should bestow the Heart Dharani and cause [the disciple] to bind the secret mudrā by means of the Vajra-bond.
Simultaneously forming the mudrā of patience and aspiration by bending the upper joints,
one should support the flower with this seal and scatter it as an offering. Then,
one should address [the deity] as follows:
This dharma-gate of the mind is the essential secret of all Tathāgatas.
Be careful not to carelessly explain it to others, for you would break your samaya.
I shall now proclaim its meaning for you.
Listen well now and reflect upon this with careful attention.
*A* signifies the meaning of non-arising;
*ra* signifies the meaning of purity, being unstained and free from the defilements of dust.
"Pa" means that even for the lame, there is no ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), as all phenomena are equal.
"Zhe" means that all phenomena possess no conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
"Na" means that all phenomena possess no intrinsic nature or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
All verbal expressions and written characters are unattainable.
Because the character *na* lacks intrinsic nature and characteristics, the character *dha* lacks all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Because the character *dha* lacks all conditioned formations, the character *pa* lacks the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Because the syllable *pa* lacks the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the syllable *ra* is free from dust and defilement.
Because the syllable *ra* is free from dust and defilement, the syllable *a* is the fundamental non-arising of phenomena (*dharmāṇām anutpāda*).
Because the syllable *a* is the fundamental non-arising of phenomena, the syllable *na* is devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
You should know this essential point:
you must contemplate that this mind is fundamentally pure and free from all defilement and attachment,
transcending the characteristics of conceptual discrimination regarding "self" and "what belongs to self."
Entering this gate is called samādhi;
it is the true practice.
One should know that such a person possesses the supreme merit certified by the Tathāgata.
Having received this Dharma,
one should perform recitation at the altar four times every day,
making offerings as described above, contemplating the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*), and entering *samādhi*.
If one recites it once, all the practitioner’s hardships and difficulties will be eliminated.
If one recites it twice, the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over billions of kalpas will be extinguished.
If one recites it three times, samādhi will manifest before them.
If one recites it four times and does not forget the dhāraṇī,
and if one recites it five times,
one will swiftly attain the realization of unsurpassed bodhi.
After reciting with single-minded devotion for one full month,
Mañjuśrī will manifest his body,
or he will expound the essentials of the Dharma within one's chamber.
At that time, the practitioner attains knowledge of past lives,
unimpeded eloquence, mastery of the supernormal powers,
and the fulfillment of supreme vows.
One shall quickly clarify the Tathāgata’s vajra-dharmakāya; or,
by drawing an image as previously described upon silk cloth,
one will also attain accomplishment after completing five hundred thousand recitations.
Alternatively, if one coats a śarīra-stūpa with fragrant mud,
writes the five-syllable mantra in Sanskrit, and circumambulates it while reciting it five hundred thousand times,
Mañjuśrī will appear before that person and preach the Dharma for them.
One shall always be protected and remembered by all Buddhas and Vajradhara Bodhisattvas.
All supreme vows will be fully accomplished.
This is the essential method for practicing the Mañjuśrī-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī.
Whenever a practitioner enters a vihāra,
they should first pay homage to the Bodhisattva at the eastern gate;
then they should pay homage at the southern gate, and likewise proceed in the same manner up to the northern gate.
Having entered the vihāra,
he faced west toward the Bodhisattva and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, single-mindedly taking refuge.
Thereafter, holding an incense burner in hand or offering exquisite flowers,
one should direct the mind to make offerings to all Buddhas and gaze upon the Bodhisattvas with a heart of joy and delight.
One should disclose all the transgressions and faults within one's own person and sincerely repent;
next, one should further praise the merits of the Tathāgata.
Having circumambulated seven times and recited [the mantra] twenty-seven times,
he again knelt on his right knee and made this great vow:
"From this day forward, having heard the *Cittabhūmi*, may I..."
"I vow not to regress from unsurpassed bodhi.
I shall extensively deliver all sentient beings, sharing in the compassionate conduct and vows of Mañjuśrī.
Having formed this thought, he sat in the half-lotus posture.
Relaxing body and mind in the serene joy of dhyāna,
he then purified both hands with scented unguents and invited the deities of the three families.
Above, below, and in the eight directions, one binds the Vajra Realm.
For the *dhāraṇī-mudrā* of the Vajra Flame Ground-Boundary: insert the *kṣānti-pāramitā* between the *balapraṇidhāna-pāramitā*, and insert the *śīla-pāramitā* between the *prajñā-bala-pāramitā*.
The *praṇidhāna-pāramitā* enters from the back and proceeds into the space between the *kṣānti-pāramitā*;
the *upāya-pāramitā* enters into the space between the *dāna-pāramitā* and the *śīla-pāramitā*.
The *dāna*, *prajñā*, *vīrya*, *bala*, *dhyāna*, and *jñāna* each touch head-to-head with one another.
Cover it facing downward;
let the wisdom fingers (the middle fingers) touch the ground like a driven stake.
Recite the dhāraṇī three times.
Visualize it as a single-pronged vajra;
the flaming vajra penetrates to the vajra-limit.
The dhāraṇī says:
Oṃ kili kili vajra-vajri phuḥ phaṭ | pūrṇa pūrṇa hūṃ phaṭ | The mudrā for the dhāraṇī of the Vajrajvālāmaṇḍala boundary is the same as the previous earth-mudrā.
Open wide the wisdom of Chan;
circumambulate to the right through the eight directions while reciting the dhāraṇī three times,
reaching as far as one desires.
Visualize a vajra-fire city with flying flames swirling like lightning.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ sara sara vajraprakara hūṃ phaṭ. The seal for the Vajra Flame Net Boundary Dhāraṇī is also according to the previous seal.
Using the wisdom-fingers of the meditative concentration mudrā, pinch the tips of the ring fingers;
rotate [the hands] three times to the right above the crown of the head while reciting the dhāraṇī three times.
Visualize vajra-flame nets extending upward to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ viśvaṃ pradarśaya vajrapañjara hūṃ phaṭ. One who performs this boundary-binding [should recite it].
The six classes of Māras and all the Vināyakas,
terrified and trembling, fled in all directions with no place to hide.
Next, the Yoga Samaya Dhāraṇī Seal is explained.
The ten pāramitās of merit and wisdom are perfected, unified, and made firm.
One establishes patience and aspiration, settling them upon the heart.
The dhāraṇī says:
Oṃ samaya saṃskṛta. Having performed this rite,
all the Buddhas recalled their original vows and,
observing and mindful [of the practitioner], bestowed the dhāraṇī-seal that opens the gate to the mind-ground.
Having performed the firm binding,
one should visualize the syllable TRA upon the right breast and the syllable THA upon the left breast.
Recite the dhāraṇī with mind and mouth in harmony.
Simultaneously scatter ten times while stroking the heart center;
part the two characters as one would open the leaves of a door.
To open their minds, the dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vajramanda traṭ. One who performs this rite [should recite it].
One will immediately be able to awaken to the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground.
Before long, one shall realize all samādhis and enter the seal of the *jñāna* (wisdom) syllable dhāraṇī. Furthermore, before that—
One contemplates a single lotus flower, red in color like crystal,
within which is the letter A;
its radiant luster is as brilliant and dazzling as a white maṇi jewel.
Having clearly seen this,
one enters into it through the firm bonds of meditative concentration and wisdom;
the power of progress is like a ring, its parts perfectly joined.
Visualize the syllables as being held within the heart.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ vajra vīśaya. Why is this so?
This very syllable *akāra* signifies the tranquil wisdom of all Tathāgatas;
it exists within the mental activities of all sentient beings yet remains unmanifested.
Now, by means of the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and skillful means, [it is revealed].
It illuminates within that [space].
Therefore, practitioners should give rise to the thought of its being difficult to encounter with earnestness,
and practice accordingly in accordance with the Dharma.
For the *Ghaḍi* (or *Ghaṭi*) *dhāraṇī-mudrā*, follow the previous method for entering the mudrā;
however, bend the forefinger (*tarjanī*) so that it rests against the back of the ring finger (*anāmikā*).
Recite the *dhāraṇī*.
Place the mudrā at the heart while visualizing the closing of a door.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ vajramuṣṭi vaṃ. For one who performs this rite:
Because one has attained the Tathāgata’s tranquil wisdom,
one should give rise to a mind of profound reverence and keep it secret;
know that such a practitioner will swiftly realize the path to tranquil enlightenment.
For the *samādhi-mukha-dhāraṇī-mudrā*, interlace the two hands with the palms facing outward and place them beneath the navel.
With the body upright and the mind focused, still all discursive thoughts.
Make each inhalation and exhalation clearly manifest.
One contemplates within the void infinite Buddhas, fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks,
as large as sesame seeds and as numerous as motes of dust,
pervading the entire dharma-realm.
One should, before each of the Buddhas,
prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground and take refuge with single-minded devotion.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāmantraṇe gṛhṇa. At that time, the Buddha snapped his fingers before the practitioner, awakening him with a sudden alertness, and addressed him, saying:
"Good son, you who have resolved upon bodhicitta should contemplate your own mind and recite this dhāraṇī, saying:"
Oṃ jitapratyaveśanakāruṇi. Having received this instruction, the practitioner leaped for joy and prostrated to all the Buddhas.
Then, reciting the secret mantra,
one visualizes the syllable *e* within the heart as being like the full moon,
not yet fully manifest, like a light mist or a cataract.
Having made this contemplation in a single moment of thought,
he addressed the Buddhas, saying: "I have seen the mind,
yet it is as if a moon that is not yet distinct."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately grant us a skillful means.
At that time, all the Buddhas praised them with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
"In this way, in this manner, I shall further empower you with this dhāraṇī so that it may become manifest.
Oṃ bodhicittam utpādayāmi. Recite this secret mantra.
Furthermore, having visualized the moon of the mind as extremely bright and pure,
one visualizes within that moon the one-syllable dhāraṇī of Mañjuśrī;
the syllable *mum* (with the second *mu* pronounced with the *han* [retroflex nasal] tone, as below) is the color of golden yellow.
It transforms into a fierce and sharp adamantine sword,
its radiance shining throughout the ten directions.
Having entered this samādhi, one further recites the dhāraṇī, saying:
Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra tiṣṭha dṛḍha. Once the moon and sword have become perfectly clear, [recite: Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra tiṣṭha dṛḍha. (The "ti" below is pronounced with the *dingyi* [ting] tone.)
Gradually cause it to expand and pervade the entire dharma-realm,
equal in measure to empty space, pure and singular without admixture,
and devoid of all marks of self and other.
This very sword is one's own body;
the observing mind resides within the sword,
and they are likewise of one essence.
The dhāraṇī for entering this samādhi is:
Oṃ sarvavajratiṣṭha tiṣṭha. Having remained according to one's strength, [one enters].
Again, he observes that the sword gradually contracts;
the Buddhas of the void enter into it accordingly,
until its size is equal to his own body, whereupon it remains radiantly still.
The dhāraṇī for entering this samādhi is:
Oṃ saṃhara vajratīkṣṇa. By the power of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas having entered the sword within the body, [it is accomplished].
He immediately transformed his own body into that of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
with a body of purple-gold color and five topknots upon his head,
and a halo surrounding his neck and back.
The left hand holds a blue lotus,
and the right hand holds a *vajra-garbha* palm-leaf manuscript; the practitioner, having already manifested as a bodhisattva,
fears that they might again become distracted and suffer a fall from their state.
Furthermore, empower it with the dhāraṇī-mudrā.
Having firmly bound the dhāraṇī-mudrā of the Bodhisattva’s three karmas,
straighten the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhi* fingers and bend their upper joints.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ nukha-cī-nā-dam. Seal it upon the heart; next, place it on the forehead and the throat, and finally on the crown of the head, reciting once for each.
Once this empowerment has been performed,
even if the mind becomes distracted, the fundamental state will not change.
All non-human beings shall behold the practitioner.
He is no different from Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and others.
The five-crested dhāraṇī-mudrā and the ten perfections are unified through precepts and wisdom.
The square of giving,
the power of patience,
and the aspects of aspiration and exertion each join their respective heads.
With both meditative concentration and wisdom held upright,
recite the dhāraṇī and seal it upon the heart, the right and left shoulders, and the throat.
Place them upon the crown of the head.
Having performed this rite while reciting each mantra once,
the Tathāgatas of the five directions will all reside upon the five topknots of the crown.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:

Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | apratihataśāsanānām | tadyathā | oṃ ra ra saṃ-ma-ra-apratihata-śāsana | kumāra-rūpa-dharīṇi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | This is the Dhāraṇī-Seal for the Consecration of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, through which merit and wisdom are perfected.
With dhyāna and prajñā entering therein,
the marks of progress and power press together like a maṇi jewel,
which is placed upon the forehead.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ ratnakuśalaye hūṃ. Having bound the jewel-garland dhāraṇī seal and performed the consecration, [the rite is complete].
Open the seal into two parts and recite the dhāraṇī:
Oṃ ratna-kuśalya-male. Circle three times above the forehead as if binding a jeweled garland.
After reaching the summit of the separation,
one again circumambulates three times to the right,
then proceeds forward and descends.
From the *Dāna-hṛdaya*, it is spread out in the manner of hanging ribbons.
This is the mudrā of the *Maitrī-karuṇā-vajra-varma-dhāraṇī*.
Firmly establish the two wisdoms.
The face of Vajra-vīrya is joined with the side [of the other].
One should visualize the syllable Oṃ on the face of Vajra-vīrya,
and the syllable Ṇa (reversed) residing in the center on the face of Vajra-bala.
It emits green light that flows without interruption, like drawing out lotus fibers.
It circles the heart three times and also circles the back three times.
Next, from above the navel it proceeds again to the back of the waist;
from atop the *paryaṅka* (cross-legged posture) it proceeds again to the back of the seat;
returning to the center of the chest, it then proceeds again to the back.
Again, it comes to the throat and returns to the neck;
then it returns to the forehead and proceeds to the crown of the head.
After circling each three times, it descends forward.
From the scattering of the wisdom of generosity, it is like a celestial robe suspended in the sky.
First, within the maṇḍala, one visualizes an image upon the heart;
therein, one contemplates the single syllable HŪṂ as a vajra-sword.
He then transforms into a true-body bodhisattva.
Subsequently, he is again invited to enter within the image.
Having firmly established the two wisdoms through the invocation of the Bodhisattva’s Vajrāṅkuśī Dhāraṇī and its mudrā;
Because he contemplates the feathers, placing them upon the feathers;
the dhyāna-wisdom (dhyāna-prajñā) hooks together,
the power (bala) is erected straight, and the progress (vīrya) is like a hook.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vartta kuśaya. Recite these three times and perform three prostrations.
The *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas shall arrive as soon as they are called to mind.
The *vajrapāśa-dhāraṇī-mudrā* is performed according to the previous invocation mudrā;
however, the thumbs and index fingers are interlocked like a ring.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vajrapadma hūṃ. Having bound the mudrā at the heart, recite the dhāraṇī three times while visualizing the Dharma-body of the Bodhisattva entering the painted image.
Having firmly established the two wisdoms for the Vajra-Chain Dhāraṇī mudrā,
extend the fingers of effort so that the right presses upon the left with their tips hooked together,
resting them against the middle joints of the back of the dhyāna and wisdom fingers.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vajrasphoṭa maṃ. For one who performs this rite, the holy one’s own body will bestow empowerment that does not dissipate.
The mudrā for the Vajraghaṇṭā-dhāraṇī follows the previous *śṛṅkhalā* (chain) mudrā;
however, the thumbs and ring fingers are each hooked back-to-back.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ vajra-gaṇḍa huḥ. By performing this rite, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and original holy ones will be completely delighted.
To offer the *argha* water *dhāraṇī* mudrā, fill an *argha* vessel with perfumed water made of saffron,
camphor, and white sandalwood; then,
opening the Buddha-family mudrā, hold it aloft in offering.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vāruṇa-khaṭa. For one who performs this offering, it is as if they were using the vajra-nectar of all Tathāgatas.
It bestows empowerment upon the crowns of the heads of all sentient beings,
eliminating the immeasurable karmic obstructions of living beings;
those who drink this water are freed from all calamities and afflictions.
The mantra for the mudrā of the hundred-syllable dhāraṇī, which follows the previous sword-mudrā,
is as follows: Oṃ keṭaṅka hūṃ ghaḥ sattva samayam anupālaya keṭaṅka hūṃ ghaḥ sattvati vīryeṇa dṛḍho bhava.
ṭiṣṭha jvala bhasma kuru me pāpaṃ muca muca pāpam anuṣṭhitaṃ me pāpaṃ sphoṭaya sphoṭaya sarva-vighnān prabhāvaya.
Yecākasarvakarmasu me citte śrīyoguru hūṃ ha ha ha ha ho bhagavan sarvatathāgatādhipate gha ma me muncāghaṭani jahi.
Recite this dhāraṇī: *mī guḥ ba va ma ha sa ma ya satva āḥ*.
This will cause the Noble One to rejoice.
The supreme vows sought for the sake of firm enlightenment shall be swiftly accomplished.
Having firmly bound the mudrā of the Vajralāsya-antar-pūjā-dhāraṇī,
raise the dhyāna and prajñā fingers straight up and place the mudrā at the heart.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ mahārati. One who performs this rite shall be as if endowed with the wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
One should make offerings to all Buddhas as a form of play.
Regarding the *dhāraṇī-mudrā* for offering within the *Vajramālā*, one uses the aforementioned mudrā and extends the arms forward,
in the manner of holding up a garland while making an offering.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ lu poṣu vi. One who performs this rite is as if making an offering with a garland of bodhi flowers.
The mudrā for the offering of the Vajra Song Dharani is the same as the previous mudrā;
it is released only after rising from the navel up to the mouth,
while visualizing according to the song.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ śrutara saukye. One who performs this rite shall be like one chanting the secret mantras of all the Tathāgatas.
And perform the offering.
For the Vajra Dance Inner Offering Dharani Seal, follow the previous seal.
Visualize it as if singing a hymn.
Upon reaching the mouth, they disperse.
One forms right-turning (clockwise) palms at the crown of the head and disperses them.
The dhāraṇī says:
Oṃ sarva-pūrye. One who performs this rite is as if making offerings with the eloquence of all Tathāgatas.
For the Vajragandha-dhāraṇī-mudrā, perform the firm *vajrabandha*,
scatter it toward the ground,
and visualize it as burning incense.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vajradhūpe svāhā. One who performs this rite offers it as if burning all manner of exquisite worldly incenses as an offering.
It enables all sentient beings to attain the fruit of coolness.
For the Vajrapuṣpa Dhāraṇī-mudrā, perform the firm binding and then scatter it upward,
in the manner of scattering flowers.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe. One who performs this rite should likewise make offerings with all manner of exquisite worldly flowers.
It enables all sentient beings to swiftly attain the full completion of the thirty-two marks.
For the Vajra-Lamp Dhāraṇī-mudrā, it is like the *hikṣi* mudrā; the dhyāna and wisdom fingers are pressed together tightly.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ vajraruci.
One who performs this rite is as if making an offering with the wisdom-lamp of all Tathāgatas.
It enables sentient beings to swiftly attain the realization of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
For the Vajra-unguent-dhāraṇī-mudrā, perform the firm bind and then scatter toward the heart.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vajragandhe. One who performs this rite shall make an offering as if with the incense of śīla-wisdom.
May all sentient beings swiftly attain the body of pure precepts.
Having performed the eightfold offerings,
cross both hands with palms facing upward beneath the navel.
As the Bodhisattva clearly contemplates and recites the five-syllable dhāraṇī,
five-colored light rays issue forth from his mouth and enter into the moon-disc within the practitioner’s heart.
Place the syllable A before oneself;
arrange the remaining four syllables in a clockwise sequence.
Contemplate the meaning of each of these five syllables one by one.
This is called the recitation of samādhi.
As for the vajra-recitation,
one relies on the previously visualized syllables.
Quickly close the lips and teeth and move the tongue slightly.
When reciting with vocal intonation, one should also visualize the form of each individual syllable within the heart;
following these syllables, the movement should be neither too slow nor too hurried.
As soon as one has caused oneself to hear it,
having recited seven times while forming the previously described sword-mudrā,
one should hold the bodhi-pearl at the heart and recite.
Perform this four times every day without interruption;
at each session, recite it one thousand times, two thousand times, five hundred times, three hundred times, or even as few as one hundred and eight times,
but do not let the number fall below this.

Even when the body is utterly exhausted, one should contemplate sentient beings in the evil destinies and redouble one's vigor in the practices of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
One should cultivate in this manner.
It should be known that the practitioner fulfills the six perfections,
realizes all the samādhis of the Tathāgatas,
and constantly has Mañjuśrī and all the bodhisattvas as companions.
This supreme admonition is difficult to predict in advance;
practitioners shall realize it for themselves.
To state the essential point: practice with diligence.
In this very life, one shall realize the first bhūmi;
after sixteen subsequent births, one shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, practitioners should reverently honor [this deity].
When one wishes to conclude, there are two methods:
first, dispatching [the deities],
and second, summoning the Bodhisattvas to enter into one's own body.
If one is performing the dismissal,
after having performed each of the eight offerings as before,
one should then recite the dhāraṇī while forming the sword mudrā.
Oṃ vajratīkṣṇa muñca— this is the mantra for dismissal.
If one is summoning a bodhisattva,
having caused them to enter one's own body by means of the four previous methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu),...
Furthermore, one should perform offerings with the eight mudrās,
don the vajra armor,
and recite the samaya-dhāraṇī.
Abiding in the four modes of deportment, he remains at ease wherever he may be.
All sentient beings, whether human or non-human,
who approach the practitioner, hear his voice and see his form.
The merit obtained from personally attending upon Mañjuśrī is such that its benefits are difficult to measure;
the most excellent matters of the world are attained spontaneously without being sought.
If one encounters persons who must be paid respect,
one should visualize that person as wearing the form of the Tathāgata upon their head,
and only then perform prostrations and kneel.
If one does not do so, one causes those sentient beings to fall into ruin and also personally violates the samaya precepts. Furthermore,
if one enters a place of sensory contact with the intent to disperse the body, [the same fault applies].
Furthermore, one should visualize the Bodhisattva entering Cāṇḍāla.
This is from the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, the Chapter on the Five-Syllable Heart Dhāraṇī of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
